content.title: Who Is Banksy, the Secret Street Artist?
content.text: Banksy is one of the biggest attractions that contemporary art has to offer today. The British street artist captivates audiences worldwide with his graffiti art, leaving his artistic mark in numerous countries. But who is Banksy really? His trademark and a significant factor in his success is his anonymity. For over 20 years, the art world has been puzzling over who might be hiding behind the pseudonym. In any case, Banksy is best understood as a one-man art project. His concept combines a mixture of street art with a simple yet striking visual language, guerrilla tactics, political messages, and a rejection of the art market. This fascinates and polarises the public in equal measure. However, it is undisputed that his works have significantly influenced 21st-century painting and inspired many imitators. Banksy's Career Began Around the Year 2000 Given Banksy's consistently secret identity, there is also no confirmed information about his biography or artistic development. It is said that he was born in either 1973 or 1974 in Bristol, where he grew up. He is believed to have learnt the art of graffiti there and started his career as a street artist. Beyond that, little is known about him. The question "Who is Banksy?" can really only be answered through his artistic activities. The art phantom Banksy first came to public attention around the turn of the millennium. As early as 1999, he is said to have shown his works in self-organised exhibitions. In the early 2000s, he began making a name for himself with his graffiti and stencil works. Over the years, his iconic works began appearing on public buildings in various countries around the world. At the same time, he occasionally participated in urban art exhibitions. He sometimes smuggled his paintings and graphics unauthorised into other artists' exhibitions. In this way, his works found their way into the MoMA in New York, the Tate Modern in London, and the Louvre in Paris, among others. Today, such semi-legal methods would probably no longer be necessary. His Projects Range from Graffiti to Major Art Actions Banksy laid the foundation for his career with street art. For many years, he has been leaving his graffiti on house walls, murals, doors, and garages using spray paint cans and self-made stencils. He often incorporates the immediate surroundings and spatial conditions into his work. Over the years, however, he has significantly expanded his range of artistic forms of expression. His portfolio now also includes works on canvas as well as prints and installations. Banksy's visual language is often straightforward and very direct. Most of his works rely on very few visual elements, such as in "Girl with Balloon", "Flower Thrower", or "Stop and Search". He frequently draws on well-known motifs and pictures for his works, modifying them sometimes more, sometimes less. In addition to his graffiti, paintings, and graphics, he has also repeatedly attracted attention in recent years through political and socially critical art projects. In 2015, these included "Dismaland", a parody of amusement parks, and the "Walled Off Hotel" in Bethlehem, which criticises the British influence in the Palestinian conflict. He also worked as a director, for example, on the now legendary and Oscar-nominated film "Exit Through the Gift Shop". Banksy's Work: Urban Art with an Attitude Banksy certainly aims to entertain, but he also sees himself as an artist with a message to convey. Many of his works subtly or overtly incorporate statements and messages about current events in politics and society. Beyond his artworks, he is also politically active and involved in social projects. For example, he supports Greenpeace and financed a ship for the NGO "Sea-Watch" to rescue refugees in the Mediterranean. He also auctioned a triptych for a Palestinian hospital, donating the proceeds of around 2.5 million euros. A consistent theme running through Banksy's artistic concept is his criticism of the mechanisms of the art market. His anonymity plays a crucial role here, preventing the widespread cult of personality and tendency towards self-promotion in the art world. Banksy also takes a different approach in many other areas of the art world. For example, he does not work with established galleries for the marketing of his works. Instead, he founded the "Pest Control Office" - an agency that handles his "paperwork". Here - and only here - can buyers authenticate his works, get in touch with the artist, and even purchase a work of art every now and then. Banksy also refuses to participate in exhibitions that charge admission fees. Who is Banksy? Three Theories About Banksy's Identity However, Banksy's real masterpiece might be the fact that he has managed to keep his identity a secret for so many years. There is very little evidence of Banksy as a private person. There is neither a confirmed name nor any photos of him. The most reliable information to date comes from a 2003 interview, in which he supposedly revealed his first name as "Robbie". In another recorded conversation from 2005, Banksy's voice can be heard. He has reportedly been spotted a few times during his spray-painting and art campaigns - but always masked or disguised. Thus, there is still no definitive information about Banksy's identity. This has led to much speculation about who might be behind the name Banksy. In recent years, three speculations have been the most persistent. Banksy's Real Name is Allegedly Robin Gunningham Robin Gunningham lives in Bristol and did not make a significant appearance in the art world until 2008. That year, the British newspaper "The Mail on Sunday" started a rumour that Gunningham was Banksy. The tabloid cited a photo allegedly showing Gunningham. In the background, stencils in Banksy's style could be recognised. In addition, the first name "Robin" points to Banksy's supposed real name, which he mentioned in an interview in 2003. Since then, Gunningham has been one of the most frequently named candidates for the "real" Banksy - though without any certain proof. Gunningham himself has remained silent regarding the speculation. Who Is Behind Banksy? Robert Del Naja Is Rumoured to Be the "Real" Identity In 2016, a journalist proposed another name that was allegedly Banksy's real identity: Robert Del Naja. Del Naja is one of the co-founders of the globally successful trip-hop band "Massive Attack". He could be Banksy's true identity, as he also hails from Bristol and has roots in the graffiti scene. The most important indication, however, is the fact that works by Banksy often appeared in locations where Massive Attack had performed. His first name Robert also fits the puzzle. However, Del Naja denied the rumours shortly after they emerged. Reports are now piling up that this lead is probably incorrect. The Rumours About Banksy's Identity Persist In addition to Robin Gunningham and Robert Del Naja, several other names have been proposed. In 2019, speculation arose that Jamie Hewlett might be Banksy. Hewlett is a British comic artist who co-founded the band "Gorillaz" with Damon Albarn in 1998. Hewlett is connected to the "Pest Control Office", Banksy's only official marketing agency. Moreover, some of Banksy's stencils appear in a Gorillaz video, and he supposedly designed an album cover. Another theory suggests that Banksy is actually Neil Buchanan. Buchanan hosted the children's show "Art Attack" on the Disney Channel in the 1990s, where kids created works of art from everyday objects. Buchanan was also a musician and was reportedly in cities where Banksy's works appeared at the same time. There is even speculation that Banksy is not a single person but a collective of up to seven artists. Ultimately, all of these theories are based on circumstantial evidence and have yet to be proven. It seems likely that the speculation surrounding Banksy's identity will continue for some time. Why Does Banksy Remain Anonymous? Banksy's anonymity is undoubtedly an important pillar of his popularity. As is often the case in the art world, Banksy's great success can largely be attributed to psychology. The idea of a phantom sneaking around the houses at night, leaving illegal murals behind, exerts a great fascination. The audience loves the game of hide-and-seek and the mystery surrounding his true identity. Almost everyone has their own theory about who Banksy might be. So, when you buy a work by Banksy, you always acquire a fragment of the myth. In addition, there is the ever-present possibility that he might cease his activities and disappear into obscurity. If Banksy's identity were revealed, he would risk a lot. He would lose his mysterious aura and become just one of many artists. This would most likely diminish public interest in his persona and, by extension, his art. Last but not least, Banksy's anonymity also protects him from prosecution, as he formally commits a criminal offence every time, he paints a wall. However, working incognito has a downside, which already prompted Banksy to change his work style. After countless attempts at forgery, he established the "Pest Control Office", where buyers can verify the authenticity of his works. Most importantly, however, the theft of his works frequently makes the headlines. For instance, the door of Paris' "Bataclan" nightclub was stolen. In 2014, Islamists had attacked the club, and Banksy had left a painting there in memory of the victims. In other cases, his works have been broken or sawn out of walls with brutal force. This has prompted Banksy to choose more surfaces for his murals that are difficult to remove. Additionally, resourceful entrepreneurs continue to exploit his name to make money. Unauthorised exhibitions showcasing reproductions of Banksy's art are held worldwide. The concept of working under a pseudonym is not new in the world of art and culture. Banksy has adopted this principle and does his utmost to maintain the game of hide-and-seek for as long as possible. The question "Who is Banksy?" will likely intrigue the art world for a while. It is not only Banksy who benefits from his anonymity. Art collectors and investors who have spent large sums on his works also have an interest in him remaining unrecognised. As long as Banksy exists only as a phantom, the art world retains one of its most interesting - and not least financially lucrative - figures.
